question: 如果发电机的发动机无法启动，我该怎么办？
reference_answer: 如果发电机的发动机无法启动，应按照手册中的故障排除流程进行检查，主要排查燃油系统和机油系统的问题。首先检查燃油系统是否正常输送燃油：确认油箱内是否有油，如果没有需添加燃油 <PIC>；如果油箱有油，请将油箱盖通气旋钮逆时针旋转1圈置于“开启”位置，并确保燃油开关旋钮置于“开启” <PIC>；若仍无法启动，可能是燃油管路或化油器堵塞，需清洁燃油管路和化油器。其次检查发动机机油系统，机油不足会导致发动机自动停机且无法再次启动：检查机油液位，如果过低需添加发动机机油 <PIC>。此外，在启动时还需注意将ECON控制开关置于○（关闭）位置，并正确操作阻风门。具体的故障排除流程可参考以下总体流程图 <PIC>。

### 漏水检查

检查水泵是否漏水，重新拧紧螺栓、螺塞、卡箍及软管接头，必要时更换O形圈及/或垫片。

question: 水泵无法抽水的潜在原因有哪些，该如何有效诊断并解决这些问题？
reference_answer:
先确认是否为“密封进气或注水不足”导致的无法抽水。手册指出，软管安装不牢固会进气导致无法抽水，且务必在进水软管末端安装滤网；每次使用前应确认泵体内水位达到上限，启动前务必向泵内注满水，否则会损坏机械密封，同时应尽量靠近水源并减少吸程。<PIC>
再逐项排查“接头与密封件松动或损坏”。若仍无法抽水，按故障排除顺序检查：注水螺塞或放水螺塞松动则拧紧；软管接头或卡箍松动则拧紧；O形圈或垫片损坏则更换；机械密封损坏则咨询经销商。
最后结合“漏水检查”进行系统诊断。日常维护中应检查水泵是否漏水，重新拧紧螺栓、螺塞、卡箍及软管接头，必要时更换O形圈及/或垫片，以恢复密封与吸水能力。

## Watercraft characteristics

Jet thrust turns the watercraft. Releasing the throttle completely produces only minimum thrust. If you are traveling at speeds above trolling, you will have rapidly decreasing ability to steer without throttle. You may still have some turning ability immediately after releasing the throttle, but once the engine slows down, the watercraft will no longer respond to handlebar input until you open the throttle again or you reach a trolling speed. Practice turning in an open area without obstructions until you have a good feel for this maneuver.
Stop the engine and remove the clip $\textcircled{3}$ from the engine shut-off switch $\textcircled{4}$ before removing any debris or weeds, which may have collected around the jet intake.

This watercraft is water-jet propelled. The jet pump is directly connected to the engine. This means that jet thrust will produce some movement whenever the engine is running. There is no “neutral” position. Keep away from intake grate $\textcircled{1}$ while the engine is on. Items such as long hair, loose clothing, or PFD straps can become entangled in moving parts resulting in severe injury or drowning. Never insert any object into the jet thrust nozzle $\circledcirc$ while the engine is running. Severe injury or death could result from coming in contact with the rotating parts of the jet pump.

## Turning the watercraft

Steering control depends on the combination of handlebar position and the amount of throttle.

Water sucked in through the intake grate is pressurized by the impeller in the jet pump. As the pressurized water is expelled from the pump through the jet thrust nozzle, it creates thrust to move and steer the watercraft. The higher the engine speed, the more thrust is produced. The amount of jet thrust, in addition to the position of the handlebars, determines how sharply you turn.

- A. More throttle produces higher thrust, so the watercraft will turn more sharply.
- B. Less throttle produces lower thrust, so the watercraft will turn more gradually.
- D. If the engine is stopped while riding, there is no thrust. The watercraft will go straight even though the handlebars are turned.

### Warning

Do not release the throttle when trying to steer away from objects: you need throttle to steer. A collision could result in severe injury or death. When operating at higher speeds, make gradual turns or slow down before turning. Sharp high-speed turns may cause the watercraft to slide sideways or spin, throwing the operator and passengers overboard, which could cause injury. EJU01080 EJU01085

This watercraft is designed to carry the operator and one passenger. Never exceed the maximum load limit or allow more than 2 persons to ride the watercraft at one time. **Maximum load:** 160 kg (353 lb) Load is the total weight of cargo, operator and passenger. Do not operate the watercraft with a passenger on board until you have considerable practice and experience riding alone. Operating the watercraft with a passenger requires more skill. Take the time to become accustomed to the handling characteristics of the watercraft before trying any difficult maneuvers. EJU01001

## Steering and sailing rules

Whenever two vessels on the water meet one another, one vessel has the right-ofway; it is called the “stand-on” vessel. The vessel that does not have the right-of-way is called the “give-way” or “burdened” vessel. These rules determine which vessel has the right-of-way, and what each vessel should do.

## Stand-on vessel

The vessel with the right-of-way has the duty to continue its course and speed, except to avoid an immediate collision. When you maintain your direction and speed, the other vessel will be able to determine how best to avoid you.
In other words, follow the standard rules except when a collision will occur unless both vessels try to avoid each other. If that is the case, both vessels become give-way vessels.

There are three main situations that you may encounter with other vessels which could lead to a collision unless the Steering Rules are followed: Meeting: you are approaching another vessel head-on Crossing: you are traveling across another vessel’s path Overtaking: you are passing or being passed by another vessel In the following illustration, your watercraft is in the center. You should give the right-ofway to any vessels shown in the white area (you are the give-way vessel). Any vessels in the shaded area must yield to you (they are the give-way vessels). Both you and the meeting vessel must alter course to avoid each other.

## Meeting

If you are meeting another power vessel head on, and are close enough to run the risk of collision, neither of you has the rightof-way! Both of you should alter course to avoid an accident. You should keep the other vessel on your port (left) side. This rule does not apply if both of you will clear one another if you continue on your set course and speed.

## Crossing

When two power-driven vessels are crossing each other’s path close enough to run the risk of collision, the vessel which has the other on the starboard (right) side must keep out of the way of the other. If the other vessel is on your starboard (right) side, you must keep out of its way; you are the giveway vessel. If the other vessel is on your port (left) side, remember that you should maintain course and direction, provided the other vessel gives you the right-of-way as it should.

## Overtaking

If you are passing another vessel, you are the give-way vessel. This means that the other vessel is expected to maintain its course and speed. You must stay out of its way until you are clear of it. Likewise, if another vessel is passing you, you should maintain your speed and direction so that the other vessel can steer itself around you.

When navigating in narrow channels, you should keep to the right when it is safe and practical to do so. If the operator of a powerdriven vessel is preparing to go around a bend that may obstruct the view of other water vessels, the operator should sound a prolonged blast of four to six seconds on the whistle. If another vessel is around the bend, it too should sound the whistle. Even if no reply is heard, however, the vessel should still proceed around the bend with caution. If you navigate such waters with your watercraft, you will need to carry a portable air horn, available from local marine supply stores.

## Fishing vessel right-of-way

All vessels fishing with nets, lines or trawls are considered to be “fishing vessels” under the International Rules. Vessels with trolling lines are not considered fishing vessels. Fishing vessels have the right-of-way regardless of position. Fishing vessels cannot, however, impede the passage of other vessels in narrow channels.

## Sailing vessel right-of-way

Sailing vessels should normally be given the right-of-way. **The exceptions to this are:**

1. When the sailing vessel is overtaking the power-driven vessel, the power-driven vessel has the right-of-way.

2. Sailing vessels should keep clear of any fishing vessel.

3. In a narrow channel, a sailing vessel should not hamper the safe passage of a power-driven vessel that can navigate only in such a channel.

## Give-way vessel

The vessel which does not have the rightof-way has the duty to take positive and timely action to stay out of the way of the stand-on vessel. Normally, you should not cross in front of the vessel with the right-ofway. You should slow down or change directions briefly and pass behind the other vessel. You should always move in such a way that the operator of the other vessel can see what you are doing. The General Prudential Rule regarding the right-of-way is that if a collision appears unavoidable, neither boat has the right-ofway. Both boats must avoid the collision.

question: When encountering vessels driving my jetski, what rules should I obey?
reference_answer:
Treat the WaveRunner as a powerboat and follow the waterway rules and regulations where you ride, including the International Rules of the Road and any local rules.

1. Know stand-on vs. give-way: the stand-on vessel keeps course and speed unless immediate collision avoidance is needed. The give-way vessel takes positive, timely action, normally slowing or changing direction to pass behind the stand-on vessel and making its intentions visible.
2. If collision appears unavoidable, both vessels must act to avoid it; both become give-way vessels.
3. Meeting head-on with risk of collision: neither vessel has right-of-way. Both alter course; keep the other vessel on your port (left) side unless you will safely clear each other on your current courses.
4. Crossing: if the other power-driven vessel is on your starboard (right) side, keep out of its way. If it is on your port (left) side, maintain course and speed as long as it yields properly.
5. Overtaking: if you pass another vessel, you are the give-way vessel and must stay clear until fully past it. If another vessel is passing you, maintain speed and direction so it can steer around you.
6. Narrow channels and bends: keep right when safe and practical. Around a blind bend, sound a prolonged 4-6 second whistle blast and proceed cautiously even if no reply is heard; carry a portable air horn for such waters.
7. Fishing vessels using nets, lines, or trawls have right-of-way regardless of position, but cannot impede narrow-channel passage. Trolling lines alone do not make a vessel a fishing vessel.
8. Sailing vessels normally have right-of-way, except when they are overtaking a power-driven vessel, when they must keep clear of fishing vessels, and when a narrow channel requires them not to hamper a power-driven vessel that can navigate only in that channel.

question: The intake and impeller of my jetski are dirty. How to clean them?
reference_answer:
Beach the WaveRunner and clean it only with the engine stopped. If weeds or debris clog the jet intake or impeller, cavitation can reduce jet thrust even though engine speed rises; if you keep running it, the engine can overheat and seize. The jet intake/intake grate area to check is underneath the hull.<PIC>
1. Stop the engine before beaching the watercraft.
2. Shut the engine off and remove the clip from the engine shut-off switch before putting your hands near the jet intake or impeller. Severe injury or death can result from contact with rotating jet pump parts.
3. Put a suitable clean cloth or carpeting under the hull, then turn the watercraft over onto its port (left) side and support the bow so the handlebars are not bent or damaged.<PIC>

5. Avoid operating where weed growth is thick. If you must travel through weeds, alternate partial throttle and full throttle, because weeds collect more at a steady speed and at trolling speed.

question: How to start my jetski in different situations?
reference_answer:
1. For every engine start, operate only in an open area. Turn the fuel cock knob to ON; use RES only if you run out of fuel, refuel as soon as possible, then return it to ON. Attach the engine shut-off cord to your left wrist and install the clip under the engine shut-off switch; the engine will not start if this clip is removed.<PIC>
2. For a cold engine, use the choke lever: direction a turns the choke on, and direction b turns it off.<PIC>
3. Press the green start switch to start the engine.<PIC> After the engine starts, check that cooling water is discharged from the pilot outlet. If the cooling passages are dry, water may take about 20 seconds to reach the outlet; if no water discharges, stop the engine and check the cause.
4. Starting/boarding in shallow water: do not start in less than 60 cm (2 ft) of water. Move the watercraft to deep enough water, board from the side or rear, attach the lanyard and clip, grip the handlebars, put both feet in the footwell, then start and move off.<PIC>
5. Starting from a dock: board from the side, attach the lanyard and clip, push the watercraft away from the dock, grip the handlebars, put both feet in the footwell, then start and move off.<PIC>
6. Boarding alone from the water: climb onto the rear platform, move to the seat, attach the lanyard and clip, grip the handlebars, put both feet in the footwell, start the engine, then look in all directions before starting off.
7. With a passenger: do not apply throttle until the passenger is seated, has both feet in the footwell, and is holding on to the operator. Start only after the passenger is secure, look in all directions, then accelerate to planing speed. If balancing at a standstill is difficult, have the passenger steady the craft while the operator boards and balances it, then start the engine and keep it at idle while the passenger climbs aboard before accelerating to planing speed.<PIC>
8. Before starting off in any situation, make sure there are no boats, obstructions, or swimmers around you. The watercraft has no brakes; do not release the throttle when trying to steer away from objects because you need throttle to steer.
